articles.headline: WNBA makes clear Enes Kanter stance after NBA player claimed to be joining women's league
keyFacts: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert told lawmakers in a letter that former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White are ineligible for the WNBA because they are men.
House Republicans had previously asked Engelbert how the league defines women and why Freedom and White would be declared ineligible.
Freedom criticized the response on social media, questioning how the WNBA determined his identity while failing to formally define what a woman is.
body: It's been a few months since Enes Kanter Freedom made headlines for being ejected from a WNBA game during his public arguments to be able to join the league.
Freedom has been at the center of WNBA controversy throughout the season, from his ejection during a Chicago Sky game, to a lawsuit afterward alleging his rights were violated.

Both Freedom and another former NBA player, Royce White, have said they declared for the WNBA Draft. But recently, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert addressed their eligibility in the most direct manner yet.
Here's what Engelbert said about Freedom and White's WNBA eligibility in a recent letter to Congress.
WNBA makes clear Enes Kanter stance in letter to Congress

Earlier in the WNBA season, Freedom and White announced plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft while saying they identify as women. The WNBA later released a statement that declared that the players "will not be used as political pawns."

In September, an inquiry from Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., and four other House Republicans about WNBA eligibility, player safety and confrontations with fans was sent to Engelbert, according to Outkick. The lawmakers questioned how the league defines "women" under Article XIII, Section 1(a) of its collective bargaining agreement and why Freedom and White would be declared ineligible.
As of Tuesday, Engelbert has reportedly responded to those lawmakers, saying Freedom and White are ineligible because they are "both men."

"With respect to your questions regarding eligibility, only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men," Engelbert wrote in a letter dated on Oct. 16, per Outkick.

In response, Stutzman said that the WNBA "has just taken the first step in defining what a woman is for the sports community," while Freedom said Engelbert "cannot clearly define what a woman is, but she's absolutely certain that I'm a man," and that "the WNBA needs to explain where it draws the line."
In a social media post, Freedom also revealed the full letter from Engelbert, where she also addressed fouls and "overly physical plays" along with the fan Code of Conduct.

🚨 LADIES AND GENTLEMEN OF AMERICA, THE MOMENT YOU’VE ALL BEEN WAITING FOR! The @WNBA has officially responded! IS THE #WNBA TRANSPHOBIC? Apparently, the WNBA still can’t define what a WOMAN is, but they’re absolutely certain they know what a MAN is! How convenient! WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert has declared that I am a man. Who gave her the authority to decide who I am? Who gets to define my identity? And how can the WNBA determine who is a man without explaining what qualifies someone as a woman? Is the WNBA denying people the right to define their own gender identity? You can’t have it both ways! America, read this letter for yourselves. THE WNBA HAS SOME EXPLAINING TO DO!
— Enes Kanter FREEDOM (@EnesFreedom) October 20, 2026

Freedom and White shared their intentions to declare for the WNBA draft in the summer, after Fever guard Sophie Cunningham spoke publicly about transgender athletes in women's sports. Afterward, the WNBA released a statement following protests by fans outside of games.

“We embrace justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion,” the statement said. “Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change. Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns.”

Freedom has also announced intentions of attending WNBA Finals Game 3 in Atlanta, per The Athletic. He was ejected from the Sky's arena, then banned, after getting into a heated exchange with Natasha Cloud during a game earlier this season.

articles.headline: LSU's RJ Luis gamble appears over: SEC denies fifth year request, per report
keyFacts: The SEC denied guard RJ Luis a fifth year of eligibility because he previously signed professional contracts, according to a report by CBS Sports.
LSU is expected to stop pursuing legal action regarding the eligibility denial, and coach Will Wade stated the program will follow SEC protocols.
LSU will open its season on November 3 while several other players await decisions on their own eligibility cases.
body: LSU men's basketball received bad news for its roster scholarship situation on Tuesday.

According to CBS Sports' Matt Norlander, former St. John's guard and 2025 Big East Player of the Year RJ Luis will not be granted a fifth year of eligibility by the SEC, and LSU is expected to back down from pursuing legal action in an attempt to make him eligible for the 2026-27 season.
He committed to LSU in May.
Men's college basketball rankings: Preseason Coaches Poll top 25 for SEC

The denial of a fifth year from the SEC is in response to Luis having signed a two-way NBA contract with the Utah Jazz and an Exhibit 10 deal with the Boston Celtics after going undrafted in the 2025 NBA Draft.

The SEC in August — at the height of fifth year of eligibility lawsuits following the NCAA's eligibility guidelines to an age-based "5-for-5" model — announced a conference policy that would prohibit an athlete from playing for an SEC member program if they previously declared for the NFL, NBA or WNBA drafts and did not withdraw from them; signed a professional contract; or were listed on a professional roster.

Luis played for Rick Pitino at St. John's from 2023-2025 and was one of the top guards in the Big East. In his junior season with the Red Storm, Luis led the team to a No. 2 seed in the NCAA Tournament after winning the Big East Tournament. He earned a second-team All-American nod after averaging 18.2 points and 7.2 rebounds per game.

"We're going to follow all the SEC protocols with him," LSU coach Will Wade said on a media Zoom call Oct. 13 (LSU did not attend SEC media days in Birmingham due to weather ). "I think it's been pretty clear what the SEC protocols are on all that. He didn't travel with us to McNeese and he hasn't been rostered."

Last week, the SEC added the Tigers' men's basketball program to its latest court filings in opposition to LSU's motion to dismiss the conference's lawsuit. The conference argues that LSU's basketball recruiting practices represent further evidence of what it characterizes as ongoing defiance of SEC professionalism rules and failure to maintain institutional control.

The Tigers' roster situation remains one of the team's biggest question marks entering the season, which begins in just a few weeks, as several scholarship players continue to await decisions in their eligibility cases.

Citing sources, Norlander also noted that 2025 NBA Draft pick Saliou Niang has been cleared to play at LSU, as Niang had not previously been enrolled in college. He also mentioned that French center Brice Dessert is expected to be cleared soon.

The Tigers list UCLA transfer Donovan Dent, one of their other high-profile portal pickups, on their official online roster , as he is eligible for now. Fellow Bruins transfer Skyy Clark is not on the roster, as his fifth-year eligibility case remains in limbo.
LSU is set to open up the season on Tuesday, Nov. 3 against LSU New Orleans at 8 p.m. ET.

articles.headline: Dave Richard's Week 7 Trade Chart and rest of season rankings: Jayden Daniels, Matthew Golden gain value
keyFacts: CBS Sports published the Week 7 Fantasy Football Trade Chart and rest-of-season rankings to help managers make fair trades.
The Trade Chart measures player values based on expected future performance, future schedules, and public sentiment rather than past performance.
Manager Dave Richard stated that managers can contact him with questions, disagreements, or trade reports via email or social media.
body: After Week 7, the Fantasy Football regular season will reach its halfway point. As long as you don't have six losses, you should consider yourself a contender. But there are two types of contenders.

If you have between three and five losses, you're probably in a win-now mindset. If you have two or fewer losses, you've probably daydreamed about making a glory run toward your league's championship.

Teams going for the gusto will attempt to land the superstar players in two-for-one and three-for-one trades from those in win-now mode. Those types of deals will begin to happen now and continue to happen up until each league's trade deadline. And while trading elite-tier superstars isn't for the faint of heart, it is an option for those who can pick up a haul in terms of quality starters in exchange.
And that's what the Trade Chart is designed to help you with.

More than fifteen seasons ago, the Fantasy Football Trade Chart was invented by CBS Sports with the sole purpose of helping managers make fair trades in their leagues. And since then, the Trade Chart has expanded to include four-point-per-pass touchdown leagues and half-PPR leagues.
Now, no one has to be scared to make a trade anymore.

The points assigned to players below reflect a long-term measurement of their Fantasy value, which is determined by expected future performance, future schedules and (perhaps most importantly) public sentiment. Past performance is not a major factor in the Fantasy Football Trade Chart.

By adding players' values, you can determine what players you should be able to get in return. However, Fantasy managers should deduct 10% of the value from any trade where one side has two or more players than the other. Also, a handful of others only carry legitimate value in two-QB or full-PPR leagues (and thus have no value listed in one-QB or non-PPR leagues).
This list also works as a "rest-of-season" rankings for the 2026 campaign.
Finally, any player not on the chart should be considered as worth no more than four points.

articles.headline: Meta suspends Muse chats sharing feature after it left private details exposed
keyFacts: Meta suspended the conversation sharing feature for its Muse AI agent after researchers exposed a privacy flaw.
Security firm Claroc found that shared chat URLs used conversation titles in subdomains, allowing public access via passive DNS searches.
Meta stated it paused the functionality to review the report and consider changes to link discoverability.
body: Meta suspends Muse chats sharing feature after it left private details exposed
Researchers accessed 6,800 shared conversations with the AI agent.

Meta debuted its Muse agentic AI platform last month and bug hunters have already uncovered a privacy problem. Users would share their Muse conversations by creating a URL, but that feature has been disabled after researchers found that anyone could potentially access those links.

Researchers at security firm Claroc discovered that the links for users' shared Muse chats can be found and accessed via a passive DNS search because all the URLs for sharing had the same domain name and used the conversation's title in the subdomain. Passive DNS are records of how human-readable domains resolve to browser-readable IP addresses, basically acting like a phone book for the Internet.

"Muse names each share's web address after the conversation's own title, and that address is written into public DNS," Claroc explained in a blog post. "One passive-DNS search brings back thousands of them, listed by name, like a table of contents."

The company was able to enumerate 6,800 links for shared Muse chats and view private information from both business and personal applications of the service. The exposed personal details included meeting times with a frontier AI lab, a small-business loan application, a bank fraud alert with partial account details, a company's vacation calendar and other internal company documents.

Ars Technica first reported on Claroc's efforts. In a statement to the publication, Meta said "we've paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered." Claroc also noted that its researchers were unable to open a sampling of the links they had previously accessed following Meta's update.

articles.headline: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
keyFacts: Google announced Tuesday that it is upgrading its in-vehicle Gemini AI assistant with a new personal intelligence feature.
The feature connects data from apps like Gmail, Calendar, and Maps to understand user preferences and answer complex requests.
The upgrade launches in Android Auto starting today and will expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.
body: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.
The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.
Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.
This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

articles.headline: LeBron James injuries, explained: What to know about sciatica, foot ailments hampering 76ers veteran
keyFacts: 76ers veteran LeBron James is managing lingering sciatica in his lower back as the season gets underway.
ESPN reported that the 76ers medical staff pays special attention to James to help him manage his lower back.
James also has chronic arthritis in his left foot that he previously played through with the Lakers.
body: By NBA standards, LeBron James is old. Even he would tell you that.

While James' ability to play at a high level — or play at all — as he approaches his 42nd birthday is just about unprecedented, Father Time is beginning to take a toll on the 76ers star in the form of some unusual injuries.
Playing on a talented 76ers team takes some of the pressure off James to be available on a nightly basis, but the four-time NBA champion is already managing some ailments as the season gets underway.
Here's what you need to know about James' back and foot injuries.
MORE: SN staff predictions for 2026-27 NBA season
LeBron James back injury

James missed the start of last season due to sciatica in his lower back, though he was able to play well and stay on the court once he returned. In fact, James was the only Lakers star fully available in the playoffs as Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves battled injuries.

Not typically a basketball condition, the sciatica is reportedly still having some lingering effects. ESPN's Dave McMenamin reported earlier in October that the 76ers' medical staff pays "special attention" to James' lower back to help him manage after last year's sciatica bout.
Here's what you need to know about the condition.
MORE: NBA win predictions for every team in the East
What is sciatica?
Sciatica occurs when nerves are compressed in the lower spine. While each case is different, sciatica typically causes pain that shoots down into the leg on one side of the body.

Lakers coach JJ Redick described James as having "nerve irritation in his glute" last season, and the discomfort was relegated to the right side for James. Based on McMenamin's report, any discomfort now appears to be focused on the lower back.
LeBron James foot injury

McMenamin also noted that James has "chronic arthritis" in his left foot, which is also not a new development. The Athletic reported James dealt with arthritis in his foot throughout his final season with the Lakers, causing him to pop up on the injury report.

While James' sciatica bout was reported to be "debilitating" at its worst, he was able to play through arthritis in his foot last season. Sciatica and arthritis aren't typical conditions that show up on an NBA injury report, but nothing about playing 24 NBA seasons is typical. At James' age, these conditions come with the territory.

As he approaches his 42nd birthday, James will evidently have to get used to managing these ailments in his first season with the 76ers. After finishing the year strong in Los Angeles, he might already be used to doing so.

articles.headline: Como vs Man United Champions League clash could be postponed amid weather warning
keyFacts: Severe rain and lightning are forecast for Como and Manchester United's Champions League match in Italy, according to weather warnings and reports.
Como officials are confident the pitch will hold up and avoid postponement, while Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick stated he is not worried.
Manchester United are preparing for the fixture after missing six players from training and seeking to end a six-match winless run.
body: Torrential rain could bring disruption to the Champions League clash between Como and Manchester United.
The misfiring Man nited have arrived in Italy for the matchday three tie on Wednesday evening, live on talkSPORT 2 at 5:45pm UK time.
Como host United on one of the biggest nights in their history, but severe weather has been forecast Getty
Como are playing in the Champions League for the first time in their history and set for their first match against an English opponent.
However, there is concern over the weather forecast just a day before the match.
Champions League weather warning
Lombardy, the region in which Como is located, has been issued with an orange warning for rain.
This is described as a severe warning of dangerous weather and there is a call for vigilance.
Rain has fallen throughout Tuesday afternoon and into the evening in northern Italy, and is set to continue until the end of the match on Wednesday.
Simon Peach of the Press Association has also reported that 64mm worth of rain is forecast before kick-off at Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia.
Only one of the four stands at the stadium are covered, which means some fans are set for very wet conditions.
Lightning could also appear around kick-off, though Como are said to be confident of the pitch holding up and avoiding postponement.
Despite the looming weather, United head coach Michael Carrick isn’t too worried about the rain.
“No, nothing immediate from me, we’re used to the rain,” he said on his potential concerns. “We’ll make the most of it!”
Heavy rain is expected to continue overnight and into the evening, with the match set for wet conditions Getty
Six players were missing from United training on Tuesday morning in what is a big blow to their match preparation.
They were said to be Ayden Heaven, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw and Patrick Dorgu.
United are looking to end their run of six matches without a win in all competitions when they face Como.
Their last European fixture ended in a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, after which Martinez called out the club board in a scathing rant .
He publicly apologised for his comments and played in the 1-1 draw at Leeds United on Sunday, although went off at half-time due to injury.
United have already picked up a Champions League win as they beat debutantes Sabah FK 4-0.

articles.headline: Democrats tout GOP stock trading ban in Texas while attacking it in Michigan
keyFacts: Two Democratic organizations are running campaign ads criticizing a Republican while praising a Democrat for supporting the same stock trading bill.
House Majority Forward targeted Republican Representative Bill Huizenga in Michigan, while the DCCC praised Democratic Representative Vicente Gonzalez in Texas.
Representative Huizenga faces Democratic state Senator Sean McCann in November, while Representative Gonzalez faces Republican opponent Eric Flores.
body: Two Democratic political organizations are running adverts on the House’s bill to ban congressional stock trading, criticizing a Republican over the vote while commending a Democrat running in a different district for supporting the bill.

The GOP-led Stop Insider Trading Act was largely opposed by Democrats as it allowed lawmakers to retain their existing stock holdings, and GOP leadership attached provisions requiring voters to show a valid ID when voting to the measure. At the time, Progressive Caucus Chairwoman Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) said it was a “sham” and “a slap in the face to the American people.”

Now, House Majority Forward and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee are both running advertisements over the legislation, with HMF running an ad in Michigan against Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-MI) over his vote supporting the measure, which passed the House in July. Huizenga is facing Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann in November.
Meanwhile, a joint ad from the DCCC and Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-TX) touts his yes vote on the same piece of legislation.
HMF’s ad depicts a man named Christopher from Kalamazoo, Michigan, accusing Huizenga of voting to keep letting corporations “keep getting rich trading stocks” and attacking his stock portfolio.

“Members of Congress are making millions trading stocks,” the man says. “Since taking office, Bill Huizenga’s stock investments have grown up to 500%. It’s like the fox guarding the hen house, apparently.”

The DCCC ad, on the other hand, calls Gonzalez a “self-made man who voted to ban Congress from trading stocks,” and cites the Stop Insider Trading Act while attacking his opponent, Republican Eric Flores.

The ad supporting Gonzalez’s vote is a change in stature for the DCCC as well, as DCCC spokesman Justin Chermol told Axios in August that “Republicans are the singular reason why a REAL ban on congressional stock trading has not become law this year,” referring to the bill.
JOSH SHAPIRO MOVES INTO THE STARTING BLOCKS FOR 2028 WITH NEW PAC
The DCCC and Gonzalez’s campaign have spent more than $450,000 on the advertisement, while House Majority Forward has spent over $800,000, according to AdImpact.
The Washington Examiner has reached out to the DCCC, HMP PAC, and Gonzalez’s office for comment.

articles.headline: Iran touts closest ever ties with Russia, contradicting Trump
keyFacts: Iran's foreign minister said ties with Russia have never been closer, while Russia's foreign minister called U.S. and Israeli attacks illegal.
President Pezeshkian stated Iran will not return to talks until the United States lifts sanctions and ends its pressure campaign.
Qatar and Pakistan presented a compromise proposal to resume nuclear talks, which sources said could yield a breakthrough this week.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Iran's foreign minister said Tuesday that Tehran's ties with Russia had never been so close, after President Trump said Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Iran amid the war in the Middle East. Russia's foreign minister, on his first visit to Tehran this week since the , called U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran illegal.

- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared a video Monday on social media of a phone call with Mr. Trump during which he suggests possible new joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, telling the American leader they have "a job to finish."
- U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth met with Netanyahu on Monday during an to Israel, according to two sources familiar with the matter.
U.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after deadly Houthi strikes

U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.

The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.

"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
Trump says he's deciding how to win Iran war: "We're doing very well with Iran"
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.

"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."

The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."

"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
U.S. must stop threats, pressure campaign before return to talks, Iran says

Iran is taking a hard-line stance on negotiations with the U.S. to end the war, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Tuesday there will be no return to talks without a halt to the pressure campaign by the U.S.

Pezeshkian met with representatives from Pakistan, including army chief Asim Munir, on Tuesday. Pakistan has played an integral role as a mediator in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, including the brief success of in June.

"(Pezeshkian) told Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir that US warmongering lies behind regional tensions, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz," according to a readout of the meeting from the official Iranian government account on X. "He said Washington must lift its pressures, threats and sanctions before any negotiations."

Those conditions are unlikely to be agreed upon by the U.S., which has , dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, over the past month. President Trump has said the economic pressure campaign has become the main strategy for ending the war.
Pezeshkian also met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Tuesday. Iran and Russia have become powerful allies.
3rd tanker hits mines crossing Hormuz strait, IRGC says
Naval mines have halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran, Iranian Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday.

"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the Guards said in an earlier statement on their official Sepah News website.
The Guards later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz."
The tanker "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems," the statement added.
Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.
President Trump has said on several occasions that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of all mines.
AFP/CBS
Iranian security chief rejects moving enriched uranium out of country
Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, on Tuesday told visiting Pakistani army chief Asim Munir that Tehran will not allow nuclear material to leave the country, according to state TV.

"Not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran. Such materials constitute a major asset and national wealth for the Iranian people, intended for use within the country," said Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
"There will be no negotiations until America takes steps to build trust — a process that must begin with the fulfilment of Iran's conditions."
President Trump has made preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon the administration's top priority.

"They can't have a nuclear weapon," Mr. Trump said Monday night at a rally in Kansas. "OK, and they won't. By the way, somebody said you could leave right now. It's true. We can leave right now. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."
AFP/CBS
Iran calls for emergency U.N. Security Council meeting over alleged bombing threat by U.S.

Iran's envoy to the U.N., Gholamhossein Darzi, sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday detailing concerns over the potential use of the so-called "Mother of All Bombs" by the United States if the war with Iran restarts after the midterms, according to state-run ISNA news.

"I wish to draw your immediate attention, as well as that of the members of the Security Council, to the recent brazen existential threats made by the President of the United States regarding the possible use of the GBU-43/B bomb, officially known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), also referred to as the "Mother of All Bombs," against Iran, as well as the renewed threats by the Israeli regime of military aggression and its declared intention to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure," Darzi wrote in his letter, according to state-owned media.

The letter from Darzi asks for Guterres and the head of the U.N. Security Council to convene a meeting and highlights four demands from the 15-country group, which permanently includes the U.S., China, Russia, France and the U.K.

Iran asks for the security council to call upon the U.S. and Israel to end their "unlawful threats" toward Iran; explicitly and unequivocally condemn threats to attack Iran; address threats to regional peace; and ensure accountability and reparations for damage from "wrongful acts committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran."

"Threatening to use the 'MOAB' bomb (the Mother of All Bombs) against Iran's civilian infrastructure and to target all of the country's energy infrastructure constitutes, among other things, a flagrant violation of international law," Darzi wrote.
Israel says army will remain in Lebanon until Hezbollah disarms, warns of further territorial seizures
The Israeli army has no plans to leave southern Lebanon anytime soon and may in fact take over more territory, according to Defense Minister Israel Katz.

"The IDF will not move out of the security zone as long as Hezbollah has not been disarmed throughout Lebanon — and the threat to the residents of the north has not been removed," Katz said on social media.
Katz also threatened to bomb part of Beirut every time an attack drone or missile was launched toward Israeli cities or kibbutzim in the north.

"We are pursuing a determined policy stipulating that any shooting or launch of drones and UAVs toward Israeli cities, moshavim, or kibbutzim will be met with a powerful response against the Dahiyeh district in Beirut," Katz said.

While Katz did say the army was willing to take more than the 700 square kilometers already below the Israeli-designated Yellow Line, it said the army would only do so if there was a coordinated attack from Iran.

"If Hezbollah joins an Iranian attack on Israel, it will be dealt a severe blow, and the IDF is prepared to carry out a ground maneuver into additional areas around Nabatieh and the Litani River," Katz said. "The territory that is captured will be evacuated of its residents, dealt with in the same manner, and permanently made part of Israel's security zone in Lebanon."
Qatar, Pakistan propose compromise to revive U.S.-Iran nuclear talks, Qatari outlet says

Qatar and Pakistan have presented Washington and Tehran with a compromise proposal aimed at preventing renewed escalation and bringing the two sides back to the negotiating table, Qatari outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported, citing informed sources.
The initiative was met with U.S. approval and a positive response from Iran, the outlet reported.

The proposal was conveyed to Iranian officials by Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who arrived in Tehran on Tuesday at the head of a delegation of Pakistani officials, according to the report.

The suggested arrangement includes a partial response to Iran's demand for the release of frozen assets. Under the initiative, Iran would receive interest generated by $6 billion in Iranian funds frozen in Qatari banks, the sources said.
In return, Tehran has reportedly agreed to an undisclosed visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency to Iranian nuclear sites, addressing a key U.S. demand concerning Iran's nuclear program.
The sources said a potential breakthrough could be announced this week.
Iran pursues legal action over U.S. torpedo attack that sank warship
An Iranian military official said Tuesday that Tehran is pursuing legal action over the U.S. torpedo attack on the IRIS Dena warship, arguing the vessel was not a legitimate military target.
In early March, Defense Secretary Pete a torpedo launched from a U.S. Navy submarine had sunk an Iranian warship in the Indian Ocean "that thought it was safe in international waters."
"Instead it was sunk by a torpedo — quiet death," Hegseth said. It was the first time a U.S. Navy submarine had used a torpedo to sink a warship since 1945.
The strike killed more than 80 Iranian service members.

In an interview with Iranian state TV on Tuesday, Brig. Gen. Moslem Yaghoubi, the Iranian army deputy for legal affairs, said the vessel was an unarmed training ship carrying trainees and that it was hit about 1,200 miles from the battlefield.
"Just this one point is enough to establish that striking it was militarily unnecessary," he said.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in June that Iran was collating documents related to the incident for what state media described as "legal follow-up," but Tehran has not specified a court in which it intends to file its legal action.
Saudi Arabia says Houthi drone and missile intercepted Tuesday
Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had intercepted a drone targeting Riyadh, as well as a missile it previously said was taken down.

Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said on X that a drone had also been intercepted and destroyed, without specifying who was believed to have launched it.

The bulletin came after the country's Civil Defense said earlier that people in the Riyadh area should "avoid crowds or going to dangerous areas, and refrain from taking photos" in a post on X, before saying the danger had passed.
Shortly after, Al-Maliki said a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis at Riyadh had been "intercepted and destroyed."
France secures 200,000 tons of extra diesel per month from UAE, Bahrain

French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Persian Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tons per month from the UAE, and an additional 100,000 tons from Bahrain, the French Elysee presidential palace said, according to the AFP news agency.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tons per month, representing just over 10% of its consumption, the statement added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France after a over soaring living costs and other social issues.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to release up to from their strategic reserves to ease pressure on global fuel supplies amid the U.S.-Iran war.

The shipments for France will be sent overland via Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, the French presidency said. Experts have questioned whether the deliveries will have an impact on prices in France, however, given the risk of renewed fighting in the region.
CBS/AFP
Iran's armed forces chief says Tehran won't wait for U.S. midterm elections to respond to any new U.S. attack
Iran's Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces warned Tuesday that Tehran would not wait for the U.S. midterm elections before retaliating to any new U.S. attack.
Maj. Gen. Abdollahi said Iran "has not waited, nor will it wait, for the results of the U.S. congressional elections" to respond to any new attack.
He blamed regional insecurity on the presence of U.S. forces and warned countries hosting American troops to remain vigilant.
"Countries hosting the United States in the region should also know that the main cause of insecurity in the region is the presence of the terrorist U.S. military," he said.
U.K. to carry out defensive air patrols over Saudi Arabia

The U.K. government announced Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia as it faces ongoing attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, including "defensive" air patrols by British Royal Air Force jets over the kingdom.

Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would "conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia, helping to protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure from Houthi attack."
He said British planes would not strike Houthi targets in Yemen.
The U.K. will also send a military transport plane and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia, Streeting said.

The announcement follows Britain's decision last month to offer in-air refueling of Saudi planes operating against the Iran-backed rebels. That mission is being extended by another 90 days, Streeting said.
CBS/AP
Death toll from Houthi attack on Yemeni military training camp rises to 73

The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 73 people Tuesday, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country began escalating three months ago, a senior Yemeni government official said Tuesday.

The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, and some were still missing a day after the Iran-backed Houthis hit the al-Alam camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, according to provincial governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir.
Qatar says Iran and U.S. still engaging, warns new escalation would push war "beyond the borders of our region"

Negotiations between Iran and the United States are ongoing despite rising tension and repeated statements from President Trump that the next month, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday.
"The negotiation is ongoing. We are seeing engagement from the parties," al-Ansari, who also serves as an adviser to Qatar's prime minister, said at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday.

Al-Ansari did not offer any further information on the negotiations, including whether there have been any recent direct contacts between Iranian and U.S. officials or if the talks are being conducted entirely via mediators.

He said discussions were continuing with regional partners and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts would eventually lead to an agreement, while cautioning that conditions on the ground were becoming increasingly difficult.
"Escalation left unchecked will mean that we are spiraling towards a regional war that will expand beyond the borders of our region," he warned.
Iran claims to have downed another U.S. MQ-9 drone and stopped 2 tankers in Strait of Hormuz with sea mines
Iran's military said Tuesday morning that it had destroyed another U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and attacked two more tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires on the unnamed ships.
In a statement, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have struck and destroyed an MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 24 American MQ-9 Reapers, two MQ-1 drones and an MQ-4C Triton the U.S. began its war with Iran, representing a loss of more than $800 million, according to a report released by the Congressional Budget Office in September.

The IRGC also claimed two oil tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iran's permission, using a southern route endorsed by the Trump administration but not recognized by Tehran, were hit by sea mines laid by the IRGC, forcing them to halt due to fires on board.

Iran has routinely targeted vessels in and near the strait for months, challenging Trump administration assertions that the vital shipping lanes are open to commercial traffic and that the U.S. military has complete control of the waterway.
At the end of August, President Trump himself declared the strait mine-free, saying U.S. forces had "totally cleared the strait of mines … Any boat goes through with a mine, we take it out."
The U.S. Navy has also struck vessels in the region as part of its own blockade of Iranian ports and associated vessels.
Pakistani army chief expected to visit Iran

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, a central figure in the country's efforts to mediate between Iran and the U.S., was expected to return for a new visit to Tehran on Tuesday, but Iran played down any hope for new wider peace talks.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said talks with Munir "relate to issues concerning the negotiations, but they are mainly focused on bilateral relations and strengthening interactions and cooperation."
The visit comes a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov made his first visit to Tehran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran.
Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," and he called the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran illegal.
CBS/AFP
Saudi forces say Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh intercepted
Saudi forces intercepted a ballistic missile that was targeting the kingdom's capital, a military spokesman said Tuesday, after authorities issued a warning for people in Riyadh to take shelter.
The kingdom "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X.

Riyadh has been targeted repeatedly by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen for weeks. Attacks on two major airports, most of them directed at Riyadh's King Khalid International, killed 20 people in one week earlier this month.
Israeli military accuses Lebanon of working with Iran-backed Hezbollah
The Israeli military accused the Lebanese army on Tuesday of working with the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in the country's south.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces said the Lebanese army "assisted efforts to prevent, delay, or thwart enforcement operations and enabled Hezbollah to prepare in advance to remove and transfer weapons from the area."

The Israeli military cited a weapons storage "asset" in Kfarra, in southern Lebanon, which it said was identified in December 2025 and flagged to Lebanese forces. The IDF said several months later, Hezbollah was still operating at the site, despite the Lebanese army claiming to have "addressed" it.

The IDF cited a between Israel and Lebanon that called for the Lebanese army to act "against the presence of weapons and military infrastructure belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in southern Lebanon."
Under that agreement, Israel was to begin transferring control of "pilot zones" in the south to Lebanese state forces in July.
The plan faced early issues, with Lebanon accusing Israeli forces of firing at its troops, while Israel said it only fired warning shots.
After a shaky start in late July, President Trump's senior Middle East adviser, Massad Boulos, told reporters "things are progressing" with the pilot zone plan, which he called a "brilliant concept."

There has been little indication of meaningful progress on the transfer of territory occupied by Israeli troops in southern Lebanon - in a "security zone" that stretches about six miles into Lebanese territory - back to Lebanese forces since the summer.
Iran signals closer ties to Russia
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Russia and Iran have never worked so closely, as Moscow seeks to present itself as a possible mediator in the Middle East war.

Araghchi hosted his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Iran on Monday — the veteran Russian diplomat's first visit to Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes on the Islamic republic at the end of February, sparking the war.

"We covered everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen. Also focused on expansion of economic and nuclear cooperation," Araghchi wrote on X. "Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."
Lavrov said ahead of his visit that Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks stalled between the United States and Iran.
On Sunday, President Trump said in a Truth Social post that "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Mr. Trump has in recent weeks , imposed over Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a bid to bring down fuel prices for Americans.
CBS/AFP
Hegseth makes unannounced trip to Israel

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes as President Trump floats resuming military operations against Iran after next month's U.S. midterm elections.

Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Russia's foreign minister condemns U.S.-Iran attacks on Iran in first visit to Tehran since war began

Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.

Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.

Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Netanyahu tells Trump "we have a job to finish" on Iran

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.

Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.
"Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."
Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
CBS/AFP
Houthis claim to have carried out 6 military operations in Saudi Arabia in 48 hours

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.

Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.

Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.

He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.

On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
AP/AFP
At least 53 killed in Houthi strike on Yemen's government forces

At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.

"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.

The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."

One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
CBS/AP
Riyadh residents receive alerts warning of "hostile aerial threat"

Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.

"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."

The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
CBS/AFP
Saudi investment conference will be pushed to 2027, its CEO confirms
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X. She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.

"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.

For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
CBS/AFP
Egyptian parliament postpones debate on military support to Saudi, state media reports

Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.

"House Speaker Hisham Badawi has adjourned the second parliamentary session dedicated to discussing authorization for taking necessary measures to support and assist the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with discussions set to resume on October 26," Egypt's state-run Al-Akhbar newspaper reported.

The postponement concluded a second day of parliamentary sessions in which Egyptian lawmakers weighed Sisi's request to approve support for Saudi Arabia, if requested by the kingdom. An emergency session on Sunday also ended without a decision.

Two lawmakers told AFP on Sunday that most parliamentarians supported the proposal, and a decision wasn't reached during that first session in order to "give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views."
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party, an opposition party with nearly a dozen seats in parliament, said it had instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting.

Although it described its solidarity with Saudi Arabia as "firm," the party said any deployment of Egyptian forces abroad should be guided by "specific objectives, clear information" and "an accurate assessment of the potential risks to the lives of our soldiers."
CBS/AFP
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claimed to have killed 558 Houthis in past 24 hours

Yemen's Saudi-backed government claimed Monday to have killed 558 Houthi fighters over the past 24 hours. In a post on X, Col. Majed Al-Nazili said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,164 operations against the Iran-backed rebels.
"The operations resulted in neutralizing (558) militia elements, including field commanders," he wrote.
Saudi investment conference to be postponed amid Houthi attacks
A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told the French news agency AFP on Monday, amid repeated by Yemen's .

One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organizers "won't announce a new date soon." A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, told AFP: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"

Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum often referred to as "Davos in the desert." The event typically draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the conference would either be held online or postponed.
CBS/AFP
Iran says U.S. responsible for insecurity in Strait of Hormuz

Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.

"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.

He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.

Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.
CBS/AFP
Iranian oil minister meets Qatari counterpart

Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA, al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
At least 50 killed in Houthi attack on Yemen government camp

The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighboring Hadramout and Aden.
CBS/AFP
Houthi rebels kill 20 soldiers, Yemen's Saudi-backed military says
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.

Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attack the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.

Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.
CBS/AP
Oil prices ease slightly as Trump softens on Russia, after attacks on ships push crude to near 5-month high
Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.

The prices fell after President to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing , with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.
Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East.
On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.
CBS/AP
Attacks continue on vessels in and near Strait of Hormuz
A tug boat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday.

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."
"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."

Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.
U.S. issues security warning to Americans in the Middle East
The U.S. issued a security alert on Monday urging Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance."

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the statement said.

It added that hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly and that groups backed by Iran may target U.S. interests overseas "or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world."
At least 20 people, including one American, were killed in one week in October when Houthi rebels attacked Saudi airports.
Russia's foreign minister expected in Iran for talks

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was expected to pay his first visit to Iran on Monday since the U.S. and Israel sparked the ongoing war with the Islamic Republic by launching joint strikes on Feb. 28.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Sunday that the two sides would discuss "regional and international developments," while Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war."
Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.

Iran presented a seven-day ceasefire proposal in late September that called for an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a return to direct negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program. President Trump rejected the proposal, which Iran says remains on the table.
CBS/AFP
Saudi-led military coalition and Iran-backed Houthis trade strikes as Yemen's civil war intensifies
Conflict raged between the Houthis and the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Iran-backed rebel group on Sunday, as both sides traded strikes.

In Riyadh, where intensifying violence has disrupted life for residents, the landmark Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered "mandatory" remote working for office tenants until further notice. Although a reason for the order wasn't provided, it followed a security alert and two drone interceptions around the capital city, in addition to a number of attacks by Houthis on Saudi targets in recent weeks.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the internationally-recognized government in war-wracked Yemen, has launched repeated air raids on regions of the country that Houthis control. One alleged Saudi airstrike in northern Yemen killed at least nine people and wounded 16 others on Sunday, the Houthis' Saba news agency reported.

The coalition said Sunday that two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed in Najran, near the Yemen border, blaming a "technical malfunction" for the incident. The Houthis said they "downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy" in the same area.
CBS/AFP
Iran says Hormuz reopening conditions still in place

Iran's foreign minister said Sunday that Tehran's conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have not changed, but that its proposal for a limited ceasefire with the U.S. to reopen the vital waterway remains on the table.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency on Sunday that Tehran is still reviewing "comments" from the U.S. on the Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that was first presented in September, but rejected by President Trump.

"If they comply with our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day," Araghchi said, referring to the timeline proposed by Iran, which calls for the U.S. to lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and to ease sanctions on the country, among other concessions.
"Our conditions are fair, and if the United States is willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, it can meet them within a few days," Araghchi said.

articles.headline: A Big Overhaul Of Xbox Game Pass Is In The Works
keyFacts: Microsoft plans to overhaul Xbox Game Pass into an à la carte model with selectable add-ons, according to Fortune and CEO Asha Sharma.
The changes aim to control costs, increase subscriber numbers, and potentially remove future first-party games from the day-one lineup.
Xbox blockbusters beginning with Fable in February 2027 suggest the overhaul will be officially rolled out before then.
body: It sounds like Microsoft isn’t done making big changes to its big subscription service. Xbox Game Pass already lost day-one Call of Duty earlier this year in exchange for a price cut, but the Netflix-like program will reportedly be getting an even bigger overhaul in the near future.

According to Fortune, CEO Asha Sharma wants to turn Game Pass from a one-price, all-you-can-eat buffet into more of an Ã la carte arrangement. The service would still be tiered but players could pick and choose which add-ons they pay for. Cloud gaming, multiplayer, and console-only games would be some of the options users can select from.

It sounds like a way to keep costs in check and grow subscriber numbers while stripping out services most people don’t use or charging those who use them a lot extra do to so. That would be in line with Microsoft’s existing testing for an ad-supported tier of Game Pass that would lower the barrier to entry for people who aren’t already diehard gamers.

But the other thing that sounds inevitable is that the rest of Xbox’s first-party games get pulled from the day-one offering. The company has already been tip-toeing in that direction for years with Premium Edition Upgrades that charge players $30 for early access to games that will be available at no extra charge just days later via Game Pass.

Leaked internal charts suggested Microsoft was once aiming for over 100 million subscribers, only for the service’s growth to plateau around 35 million and the entire business model around Xbox this console generation to unravel as a result. The next batch of Xbox blockbusters begins in February 2027 with Fable. My guess is that this reported Game Pass overhaul gets officially rolled out sometime before then.

articles.headline: Next Xbox console reportedly coming in 2028 and could cost as much as $1,800
keyFacts: A Fortune report citing internal projections states that the next Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, could cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it launches in 2028.
Fortune reports that Xbox is planning to release a new handheld next year and a major overhaul of Game Pass with a tiered, a la carte structure.
CEO Asha Sharma said that business is rebounding with recent changes during her first few months since taking over.
body: This mess of a console generation for Xbox is rapidly coming to an end, and the state of the industry is spelling out more horror for gamers on the horizon.

New CEO Asha Sharma says things are turning around in her first few months since taking over, with the business rebounding with some recent changes. But according to a new report from Fortune , the good vibes will come to an end when the next console’s price tag is revealed.

Image via Xbox Citing internal projections, the report states that the new console codenamed Project Helix could cost between $1,200 and a whopping $1,800 when it launches in its currently scheduled period of 2028, “unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.” That’s a number that could get you a pretty decent gaming PC. Or, at least it used to. With how component prices continue to horrifyingly rise, who even knows anymore.

This news follows up a weekend report from WCCFTech that Sony’s next console, Microsoft’s main competition for the Xbox that’s also spent this generation making poor decision after poor decision, will also come in at well over four digits. The cost of producing the RAM and SSDs necessary for the presumed PlayStation 6 has already reportedly reached around $680, and is likely to climb. So, yeah, get those payment plans ready.

To pair with the Helix console, Fortune says Xbox is planning to release a new handheld next year ahead of the console in 2028. The company is also working on “a major overhaul of Game Pass that would have players choose features à la carte, including add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer, with the system operating on a tiered structure.”

With how prices are looking for gaming in general, I’m beginning to understand what the company was trying to go for with its “This is an Xbox” slogan and ad campaign (not really). But now, you’ll need to probably fork over an entire average paycheck (or more) to play whatever game the company is working on next.

articles.headline: Gavin Newsom saddled Californians with $14B in new taxes in final years as governor: report
keyFacts: Governor Newsom and Democratic lawmakers approved measures raising California taxes and fees by $14.3 billion annually, according to a report.
Two budget measures targeting software sales and health plans drive roughly 80 percent of the increases, according to the report.
The California Tax Foundation said these costs will raise living expenses as a new governor takes office facing affordability problems.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom loves to rattle off statistics — but he may not like a whopping new figure being tagged to him and California Democrats ahead of his likely presidential campaign.

Democratic lawmakers and Newsom have approved measures during the last two-year legislative session that will raise taxes and fees by an estimated $14.3 billion annually, according to a new California Tax Foundation report.
The increases come as Californians already pay the nation’s highest gasoline taxes, highest statewide base sales tax rate and highest top personal income tax rate.

“When the new taxes and fees approved this session are fully implemented, Californians will be paying $14.3 billion more to their state and local governments, on top of any additional taxes approved in the November election,” California Tax Foundation research analyst Caitlin Herring said in a statement.
“These new expenses will increase the cost of living in this state just as a new governor takes office and begins grappling with California’s ongoing affordability problem.”

A back-of-the-envelope calculation would suggest the taxes would be a roughly $1,000 annual increase per California household, but the tax foundation cautioned that most of the taxes target specific taxpayers and businesses.

The foundation’s analysis identified 156 proposals to increase taxes or fees during the 2025-26 session. Of those, 67 passed the Legislature and were signed into law by Newsom. The approved increases represent a fraction of the more than $803 billion in proposals lawmakers considered, according to the report.
Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Earlier this month, the California Medical Association and the California Association of Health Plans said a new state health care tax — expected to raise family premiums by hundreds of dollars annually — violates Proposition 35, a 2024 measure approved by 68% of voters that set limits on such taxes.
The two largest increases came from proposals Newsom incorporated into the state’s 2026-27 budget, according to the foundation.

One measure, Senate Bill 122, extends taxation to sales of digital prewritten software regardless of how customers receive it. That includes Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), where the customer accesses the software hosted by the vendor but never takes possession of it.

The same legislation limits businesses’ use of tax credits, increasing the amount employers owe. Together, the changes are projected to generate at least $9.17 billion annually, according to the report.
A second budget measure, Senate Bill 125, imposes a health plan tax that the foundation estimates at $2.3 billion annually.
Combined, those two measures account for about $11.47 billion, or roughly 80% of the annual increases identified in the report.
The foundation also tracked how much individual legislators supported higher taxes and fees through their votes.

Assemblymember Robert Garcia (D-San Bernardino) backed measures totaling $795 billion, the highest amount in the Assembly, while Sen. Lena Gonzalez (D-Long Beach) led the upper chamber at $790 billion, according to the analysis.
