articles.headline: Vance reveals the Trump dilemma that could complicate his 2028 White House ambitions
keyFacts: Vice President JD Vance said he is uncertain whether Donald Trump would immediately endorse him if he runs for president in 2028.
Vance stated that Trump's endorsement carries significant weight with voters because it signals opposition to party elites.
Vance emphasized that his top priority is the upcoming midterm elections rather than a potential 2028 presidential run.
body: Vice President JD Vance said he isn't sure if he'd receive President Donald Trump's endorsement "right out the gate" if he were to run for president in 2028.

Vance expressed that uncertainty during a Monday interview with journalist Mark Halperin on his platform 2Way. The interview aired just weeks before the midterm elections, as Republicans and the White House are focused on maintaining control of Congress.
Vance emphasized that his top priority was the midterms and said he wasn't certain that a 2028 presidential run was in his future.
However, he said, "I think if I run, the president will endorse me."
VANCE CONFRONTED ABOUT 2028 AMBITIONS AFTER TRUMP TEASES 'DREAM TEAM' RUBIO TICKET
"Right away?" Halperin asked.
"I would think so, but I don’t know, man," Vance said. "I haven’t talked to him about it."
Halperin suggested it might be "weird" if Vance were to share with Trump his 2028 ambitions and for Trump to sit on an endorsement, a characterization that Vance pushed back on.

"No, I don’t think it’d be weird," Vance said. "Again, I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race, and because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let, like, this race play out and not, like, preemptively prejudge the results.'"

Earlier in the conversation, Halperin brought up previous remarks by Vance in which he said that "whoever the president endorses for the Republican nomination will ultimately win the Republican primary."
CRUZ-VANCE RIVALRY HEATS UP AS TEXAS SENATOR SUGGESTS VP IS 'FEELING INSECURE'

Vance said this is typically true of both the Democratic and Republican parties, but that Trump's endorsement is much more consequential because he first won the trust of everyday voters while Republican Party elites rejected him. Vance said Trump's endorsement signals to voters that a candidate is not beholden to the party's elite.

"That’s the person they say, ‘Okay, if Trump is with a guy, that must mean that the elites are against that guy," Vance said. "I think that Trump’s endorsement just carries more weight than any political endorsement in history because of that. Obviously, the voters are gonna decide. Donald Trump is only one vote of many, but I think his endorsement is still the most powerful."

Vance's uncertainty over winning Trump's blessing comes after Trump previously teased pitting Vance against Secretary of State Marco Rubio for his endorsement in the 2028 presidential race. Trump called Vance and Rubio the "dream team," at a May Rose Garden Club event but has refused to say who would be at the top of the ticket.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met European leaders and US envoys in Oslo to discuss peace efforts amid US-Ukraine tensions.
Finnish President Stubb said US envoy Steve Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to discuss ideas with Russian leaders.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has resumed receiving early intelligence warnings from partners about incoming Russian strikes following a call with Marco Rubio.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration.
Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace'

During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely.
Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference.
"US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said.
Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting.
The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles.
Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume
Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders.
There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues.

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table.
Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel. Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine.

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks.

Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine.
At a recent European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump.

The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office.
In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand.

Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces.
"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.

articles.headline: Trump says he hasn’t spoken to Vance about a 2028 endorsement
keyFacts: President Donald Trump stated Tuesday that he and Vice President JD Vance have never discussed a potential 2028 presidential endorsement.
Vice President JD Vance stated in a recent interview that he has not decided whether to run in 2028 and is currently focused on the midterm elections.
President Trump stated that it is too early to discuss 2028 endorsements because the focus must be on the midterm elections.
body: President Donald Trump would not say if he will endorse Vice President JD Vance for the presidency in 2028, telling reporters Tuesday that the two men have never discussed the topic.

“He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person, but we’ve literally — I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” Trump answered Tuesday in the Oval Office when asked about Vance’s recent comments that if he ran, the president would back him.

Vance is widely viewed as the heir-apparent to the president’s MAGA mandate, and he’s been pulling double duty during the 2026 midterm cycle, serving as the Republican National Committee’s finance chair and top surrogate. But Vance has steadfastly avoided publicly discussing the possibility of running in 2028. He previously told the Washington Examiner that he would wait until after the midterm elections before even contemplating a bid.
Earlier this week, Vance told Mark Halperin during an interview that he had yet to make a decision on running in 2028.

“I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven’t focused on it,” the vice president said. “You and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me, sure.”
Vance said during the interview that he hadn’t broached the topic with Trump and was focused on helping Republicans win the midterm elections.
“I think if I run, the president will endorse me,” @JDVance told @MarkHalperin when asked today about 2028. pic.twitter.com/2djXrd6LVY
— 2WAY (@2waytvapp) October 19, 2026

Trump struck a similar tone in the Oval Office on Tuesday.

“We are very early right now,” said the president. “We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes. I’m going to a rally in North Carolina. We had an amazing rally last night, Kansas, for a tremendous person.”

articles.headline: Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’
keyFacts: Democrat Adam Hamilton is challenging incumbent Republican Roger Marshall in a Kansas US Senate race that is too close to call.
A win by Hamilton would be historic, as Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932.
Hamilton is pitching himself as an independent-minded Democrat to win over independent and Republican voters across the state.
body: Just two years after Donald Trump won Kansas by 16 points in his fight to regain the White House, Republicans in the state are scrambling to retain their dominance. The battle for one of its two seats in the US Senate is too close to call, setting the stage for a potentially extraordinary upset.
Some recent polls even put Democrat Adam Hamilton on course for a historic victory. Kansans have not sent a representative of the party to the US Senate since 1932.

On the campaign trail, Hamilton regularly points to one of his state’s most famous residents: Dorothy from Wizard of Oz. Recalling a visit he made to Liberal, Kansas, and its Oz museum, he asks the audience to recall what Dorothy’s companions on her journey need. The lion needed courage, the scarecrow a brain and the tin man a heart.

Washington needs more of all three, he says, and he can deliver it. He decided to run for office after seeing the Trump administration act in ways that were “not good or kind or compassionate or humble”, Hamilton – in the energetic cadence of the pastor he is – told a crowd of business leaders in Topeka on Friday. He was waiting for Roger Marshall, the state’s Republican incumbent senator, to stand up for his state and its people.

“I would have arguments with Roger Marshall in the shower. He was not in the shower with me,” Hamilton joked. “And I would just say, Roger, please stand up for your people. You were not hired to be a spokesperson for the White House. You were hired to fight for your people.”

Hamilton’s role as senior pastor of the country’s largest United Methodist congregation comes with name recognition and speaking skills. But Marshall’s liabilities as his opponent – namely, the fact he sued hundreds of his patients for unpaid bills, resulting in the arrests of dozens of them – have contributed greatly to Hamilton’s prospects of flipping the seat.

He readily and frequently shares the stories of everyday Kansans he’s met on the trail for US Senate, from the woman whose health insurance premiums cost as much as her mortgage, so she had to drop coverage, to the farmer who cried over the state of the industry for young farmers.

Electorally, he’s trying to win over independents and Republicans, calling himself an independent-minded Democrat. It would be valuable, he told the business leaders last week, for Kansas to have a Democrat like him and a Republican in Jerry Moran representing them in the US Senate – working both sides of the aisle.

In a video welcoming Trump to Kansas, Hamilton said he hoped the president would hear from the people struggling throughout Kansas with rising costs and uncertainty. But, he told Kansans, they all had a place in his campaign, regardless of who they voted for, or their party affiliation.

“I’m running to be a champion for the people of Kansas: Republicans, Democrats and independents. I won’t answer to a party, and I won’t answer to any one person in Washington,” he said in the video. “I answer to you.”

In Topeka, Kansas voters were open to the pitch. Several who attended Hamilton’s forum on Friday had attended a similar forum with Marshall earlier in the day. Before and after the event, Hamilton circulated through the crowd of a few dozen voters, shaking hands and taking photos. Voters said they appreciated his accessibility, even if some wanted some more specific answers.

Brennen Ross, a 20-year-old political science and economics student at Washburn University in Topeka, watched Marshall earlier in the day then came to see Hamilton. The national attention on Kansas now has been “super interesting” for a state often best known for its sports teams, he said.

He’s an unaffiliated voter, leaning toward Hamilton. The cost of housing, the job market for people his age and the availability of water in rural Kansas are all weighing on his mind, he said. The first issue he mentioned, though, was Hamilton’s effort to “turn the heat down” amid rising political polarization.
“That’s really compelling, and it resonates with a lot of Kansans, especially like a lot of younger Kansans that I speak to on this election,” Ross said.

Jacinta Bergkamp, a 30-year-old Democrat with a young professional group called Forge Young Talent, asked both Hamilton and Marshall about housing affordability at each of their events. She said affordability looms large across the board for young people. Women’s rights and access to abortion matter to her vote, too.

Bergkamp, wearing a shirt that said “Vote Dammit”, has found the Democratic interest in Kansas “encouraging” and said that Kansans have seemed “fed up” with what they’re experiencing, with more people willing to speak out against their representatives and hold them accountable.

“Usually it feels a little, I guess, lonely” to be a Democrat in Kansas, she said. “We always kind of think of Kansas as being purple. Kansas isn’t red or blue … It’s very clear that Kansas is more liberal than what people think outside of Kansas.”

Linda Murphy Maina, who owns a Topeka boutique called Linda’s Afrikan Kreations, said she looks for which candidates are good for the people, and how they can serve the community. On some questions, she wanted more direct answers, but she felt Hamilton homed in on working together and helping people. “I’m still doing a little research, but he tickled my fancy,” she said.

Susana Ortiz, a counselor who has a private practice in Topeka, said her background in mental health meant she looks for candidates who would be best for her clients. She doesn’t expect candidates to have all the answers, but they need to show they care about people, and are willing to accept feedback from the public about their decisions.

Ortiz is still deciding who to vote for. “More and more people, it seems, are expressing frustration with the rising cost of living,” she said. “And so they’re looking for solutions, and I think that allows people to be a little more open-minded to perhaps voting across party lines.”

Hamilton, working to convince the politically mixed crowd to take a chance on a Democrat, told the Topeka business leaders that he didn’t think Marshall had done a good job of listening to the people. He noted that the last time Marshall held an open town hall was about 600 days ago, when he left the town hall after facing pointed questions. (Marshall has said the town halls became “non-productive and dangerous”.)

Hamilton doesn’t have many superpowers, he told the crowd. He can’t sing, he’s bad at golf, he was a horrible football player. His superpower, he said, is that he listens and he really cares, and he has a “propensity to fight for people”.
“I’m gonna just fight like hell for the people in Kansas,” he said.

articles.headline: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
keyFacts: A US district judge dismissed a lawsuit against OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman brought by his sister Ann Altman.
Ann Altman claimed Sam Altman sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006, accusations he and his family denied.
Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the case because Ann Altman failed to attend a medical examination.
body: - Published
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.
A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.
Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.

District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".

"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.
The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.
In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.

However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.
The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.
The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".
Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.
If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

articles.headline: The Supreme Court is about to decide whether to ban trans women from women’s sports
keyFacts: Plaintiffs filed a Supreme Court shadow docket case seeking to bar transgender women from competing on women's school sports teams nationwide.
A high school wrestler sued after alleging sexual assault by a transgender opponent, but prosecutors declined to charge, citing insufficient proof.
The Supreme Court will decide whether to intervene, while the school district said its investigation into the match remains ongoing.
body: The plaintiffs in the case K.M.K. v. Washington Interscholastic Activities Association effectively want the Supreme Court to bar trans women from women’s sports teams at high schools and universities. | Heather Diehl/Getty Images

One of the last decade’s most consequential changes to how the Supreme Court operates is the growth of the so-called shadow docket — a process that allows the justices to decide cases unusually quickly, and often without full briefing or oral argument.

Historically, the Court would typically allow contentious legal issues to percolate in the lower courts for months or even years before the justices agreed to decide one of those issues. Then they’d spend months reading briefs, hearing arguments, and debating the case amongst themselves before they finally issued an opinion. This slow process existed because the Supreme Court is the final word on many legal questions — the Court can even override Congress if it claims a law is unconstitutional — and so it should be cautious before it hands down a decision that cannot easily be displaced.

A new case, which recently arrived on the Court’s shadow docket, embodies all the reasons why America’s highest Court should act carefully and slowly. K.M.K. v. Washington Interscholastic Activities Association involves a highly contentious issue — the plaintiffs in the case effectively want the Supreme Court to bar transgender women from women’s sports teams at high schools and universities, even in states that support trans inclusion in sports.

It also involves an appalling sexual assault allegation. One of the plaintiffs in the case is a high school women’s team wrestler who is identified only by her initials because she is a minor. She claims that one of her wrestling opponents, who is transgender, “forcefully” penetrated the plaintiff’s vagina with her fingers during a match.

As a memo from the local prosecutor’s office points out, if these allegations are true then K.M.K. is the victim of a very serious crime — rape in the third degree . The prosecutor’s office, however, decided not to prosecute because it concluded that it could not prove that a sex crime was committed beyond a reasonable doubt. Among other things, prosecutors spoke to the referee who officiated the match, and he said that “nothing stood out to him during the match” and that “after watching the video of the match, he could not say that the suspect’s hand placement was ‘anything out of the ordinary.’”
The school district, meanwhile, says that it has reviewed video of the match, interviewed both competitors, and that its investigation into the allegation is “ still ongoing .”

K.M.K. , in other words, is exactly the sort of case that the justices should step away from, sending it back down to the lower courts to gather more information and to fully think through the difficult legal issues presented by the case. Setting aside the horrifying allegations against her one-time opponent, K.M.K.’s lawyers — most of whom work for a Christian right law firm , the Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) — make novel legal arguments that ask the Court to make broad pronouncements that go far beyond its previous precedents.
One of their arguments, if taken seriously by the justices, could potentially make it impossible for any school athletes, whether cis or trans, to participate in competitive sports of any kind.

There is a very real risk, in other words, that the Supreme Court will, if it moves too quickly in this case, harm millions of school athletes throughout the country. The factual question of whether a particular wrestler committed a crime is separate from the legal question of whether federal law strips states of their authority over trans participation in women’s sports. And this legal question deserves more deliberation than the Court can give it if it decides this case on the shadow docket.
So what are the actual legal issues in K.M.K. ?

In West Virginia v. B.P.J. (2026), the Supreme Court warned that judges should not be given the power to decide which athletes may compete on a women’s sports team. “The legislatures and the schools are better equipped — and under the Constitution, are the more appropriate entities,” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote for his Court, “to assess the competing medical and scientific considerations and draw appropriate lines.”

B.P.J. , of course, was a loss for transgender rights . The Court rejected a constitutional challenge to state laws that forbid trans women from playing on school sports teams within that state. But the legal question in B.P.J. was whether laws barring trans women from women’s sports are allowed — a question that the Court’s Republican majority answered in the affirmative. A victory for the plaintiffs in K.M.K. , by contrast, would likely establish that no state may permit trans women to compete on women’s sports teams, regardless of what the people of that state want.

This Court is often skeptical of claims by trans rights advocates , and it almost always resolves disputes between cultural liberals and religious conservatives in favor of the religious right . That said, this Court has thus far respected states’ rights on another contentious issue that is a high priority for the religious right: abortion. Although the Court’s Republican majority overruled Roe v. Wade and eliminated the constitutional right to an abortion, it has rejected some attempts to restrict abortion in blue states — including by repeatedly ruling against litigants who seek to ban the abortion medication mifepristone .

So it is, at least, possible that this Court will follow a similar path in K.M.K. and conclude that the question of which team trans women should play on should be answered by the states and not the Supreme Court.

Broadly speaking, ADF raises two legal arguments against Washington state’s policy allowing trans women to play on women’s sports teams. It claims that Title IX , a federal law that bars “sex” discrimination by most schools, implicitly requires those schools to have sports teams that only cisgender women may play on. It also claims that the Court’s recent decision in Mirabelli v. Bonta (2026), which requires public schools to out trans students to their parents even if the students wish to keep their gender identity secret, also requires those schools to exclude trans women from women’s sports.

There’s no reason for the Supreme Court to decide either of these questions now, however. As Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in Lux v. Rodrigues (2010), when a party that lost in the lower courts seeks an injunction from a Supreme Court justice before their case is fully litigated in those lower courts, they must demonstrate that “the legal rights at issue are ‘indisputably clear.’” This rule, like many old rules disfavoring shadow docket decisions, exists to prevent the justices from rushing into a decision that may later prove unwise.

There is no plausible argument that Title IX “indisputably” bars trans women from women’s sports. That’s because, just a few months ago in B.P.J. , the Court held that it was not deciding the question of “whether, under Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause, schools may allow biological males who identify as female to participate on girls’ and women’s sports teams.” So that’s a recent Supreme Court precedent holding that the answer to this legal question remains open.

Mirabelli , meanwhile, is an unusually thinly reasoned decision. The Court’s Republican majority held that schools must out trans students because of a judicially created doctrine saying that parents have “ primary authority with respect to ‘the upbringing and education of children.’ ” But the Court’s analysis of this issue was just a single paragraph long, it relied on the most malleable doctrine in all of US constitutional law , and it had nothing to say about sports.

Moreover, as the school district points out in its brief, the Court has never held that a parent’s right to direct the upbringing of their child includes a right to dictate which rules will be used by school sports teams . If such a right existed, a parent might insist that a school bar players of a particular race. Or they might demand that their child be allowed to play football without being tackled.
Competitive team sports simply cannot exist if one player’s mother is allowed to demand changes to the rules that neither the league nor the other players support.

In any event, at this stage in the litigation it should be enough for the Court to say that the unique right claimed by K.M.K.’s mother — the right to dictate which rules a multischool competitive sports league will use — is not “indisputably clear” under current law.
What should happen when the Court eventually decides whether blue states may allow trans women to play on women’s teams?

It is, to borrow from Lux , indisputably clear that the Court should not give the K.M.K. plaintiffs the sweeping policy change that they seek in a shadow docket ruling. But the justices cannot avoid, forever, the question of whether federal law forbids trans women from playing on women’s teams. So how should they resolve this question when it is more properly presented to them?

Let’s dispose of the plaintiffs’ Mirabelli argument first. While the Court has held that parents have some right to direct the education of their children, prior to Mirabelli , this right was construed narrowly. One older case held that states may not forbid parents from sending their children to private schools . Another held that the government may not bar teachers at these schools from teaching the German language .

Prior to the Court’s barely explained decision in Mirabelli , however, the Court had never held that parents may dictate how public schools operate, and the school district’s brief in K.M.K. cites several court decisions warning against giving parents too much authority over public schools. (The Court did hold, in Mahmoud v. Taylor (2025), that parents who object to a school’s curriculum on religious grounds may opt their children out of certain lessons. But the K.M.K. plaintiffs do not raise a religious objection.) As the Supreme Court said in Prince v. Massachusetts (1944), states may “restrict the parent’s control by requiring school attendance, regulating or prohibiting the child’s labor and in many other ways.”

It’s clear from Mirabelli that the Court’s Republicans do not share this caution about judicial control over public schools. But, because Mirabelli was so thinly reasoned, it’s also impossible for outside observers to determine why these justices want an unprecedented amount of control over public schooling, or whether they have good reasons for asserting this new power.

I will simply reiterate the school district’s objection that, once the Supreme Court opens the door to parents dictating which rules will be used in school sporting competitions, the lawsuits will not end with parents seeking to kick trans women out of women’s sports. The next parent may object to their child wrestling Black people. Or they may demand that their child be given protective gear that gives them a competitive advantage. Some parents may also demand rules changes that conflict with changes demanded by other parents. And there is no principled way to distinguish these requests from a request to exclude trans women.

There are myriad problems, meanwhile, with the K.M.K. plaintiffs’ Title IX argument. That statute provides that schools that receive “Federal financial assistance” may not exclude individuals from “any education program” on “the basis of sex.” This statute has long been read to require equal treatment of men’s and women’s sports by schools that receive federal funds.

But, as the school district argues in its brief, Washington schools do not discriminate on the basis of “sex” — which the Court has defined to mean sex assigned at birth in this context. Instead, they classify athletes on the basis of gender identity. There is one team for all people who identify as male, whether trans or cis, and another team for all people who identify as female. Social conservatives may object to this arrangement, but it does not classify students based on their sex assigned at birth at all.

The K.M.K. plaintiffs’ argument is also undermined by federal regulations implementing Title IX. Those regulations provide that schools generally should not separate women and men in sports, but that they “ may operate or sponsor separate teams for members of each sex where selection for such teams is based upon competitive skill or the activity involved is a contact sport.” It is quite a stretch to read regulations saying that schools “may” have sex-segregated teams to say that schools must ensure that their teams are strictly sex segregated.

Finally, recall that Title IX only applies to schools that accept federal funding — schools have the option of rejecting Title IX’s requirements if they also forego federal grants. This matters because, as the Court recently held in Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections (2026), “Congress must clearly and unambiguously alert a grant recipient to any condition on federal funds.”

Thus, if there is any ambiguity about whether Title IX requires schools to exclude trans women from women’s sports, that ambiguity must be resolved against imposing any requirements on public schools. Title IX may only be read to ban trans women from women’s sports if it “clearly and unambiguously” does so.

Again, there’s no reason for the justices to resolve either of these questions because, at this early stage in the litigation, the Supreme Court should simply decline to decide K.M.K. because the plaintiffs’ legal rights are not “indisputably clear.” But this Court is often impatient, especially in cases involving culture war issues . Mirabelli was also a shadow docket case, but that didn’t stop the Court’s Republicans from inventing a new legal rule compelling teachers to out their trans students .

There’s a serious risk, in other words, that this Court will rush to decide K.M.K. before it fully considers the legal arguments on either side, or even learns whether the genuinely shocking allegations raised by the plaintiffs have merit.

articles.headline: Next-Gen Xbox Could Be $1,800 And Launch In 2028 – Report
keyFacts: Fortune reported that Microsoft's Project Helix console could cost between $1,200 and $1,800 and potentially launch in 2028.
The report stated that Microsoft might also release a next-generation Xbox handheld device by the end of 2027.
According to Fortune, more Xbox layoffs are scheduled to occur this month, in November, and in January 2027.
body: A new report sheds more details on Microsoft's plans for new Xbox hardware, including a new handheld device and console, and one of the biggest takeaways is the alleged price.
According to Fortune , the Project Helix console could cost between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft opts to subsidize the cost. The system could launch in 2028, the report said.

It's not uncommon for platform-holders to eat some of the cost of a new console and make up the difference with software and services. When the Xbox Series X and S platforms launched in 2020, then-Xbox CEO Phil Spencer said Microsoft was losing as much as $200 on every console it sold.
Project Helix might be very expensive.

Part of what might be driving up the price for new consoles is the ongoing AI-fueled memory and component shortages. Microsoft itself is one of the biggest proponents of the build-out of all things AI, so its own efforts are contributing to an environment where the next Xbox could be incredibly expensive. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reacted to this irony, saying it's "wonderful" that GPUs have use beyong gaming.
Richer households already made up the majority of console-buyers today , and that trend is expected to continue
Additionally, the report said Microsoft might release a "next-generation handheld device" for Xbox by the end of 2027, though there were no details on pricing or anything else.
Project Helix is the name for Microsoft's efforts for a "family of devices," so that would seemingly span both console and handheld.

The report added that Microsoft's Xbox and Windows teams reportedly battled over what software should run Project Helix, with the Windows team wanting the handheld to use a "trimmed-down" version of Windows Home. The Xbox team, meanwhile, reportedly pushed to build its own dedicated software.

An unnamed "senior Xbox executive" was said to have threatened to pull the plug on the entire handheld device rather than use Windows. Going forward, Xbox is "largely controlling the direction" of the handheld's OS, but Sharma told the site that the two teams work together. "We can't build Helix on our own," she said.

Sharma took over as Xbox CEO in February this year, immediately declaring that Xbox was in an unhealthy place and taking drastic measures that she believes may right the ship, including laying off staff, closing studios, and cancelling games. The layoffs, which have included about 2,000 people so far , are not done yet, as the Fortune story says more Xbox layoffs are coming this month, in November, and then again in January 2027.
Sharma also made major organizational changes, including handing Halo over to Activision for the future .

articles.headline: As Midterms Approach, Top American Fears Include AI Interference in the Political Process
keyFacts: Chapman University published its annual survey revealing top American fears for 2026, which included artificial intelligence for the first time.
Researchers found that AI interference in the election process ranked third and economic harm ranked seventh among American fears.
Corrupt government officials remained the most central fear for Americans at 61.1%, according to the survey results.
body: Are you more fearful of AI stealing jobs, hurting the economy and disrupting the political process than you are of someone you love dying? A lot of people are, according to Chapman University’s 12th annual survey on American fears for 2026.

This year’s survey by the private research university in California was different. For the first time, researchers began asking Americans about their thoughts and fears about artificial intelligence, and those AI-related fears made the top 10 twice, as well as popping up throughout the list.
These were the top fears in the minds of the American people for 2026.
More from CNET

The most central fear for Americans has remained unchanged since last year: corrupt government officials, at a staggering 61.1%. Other common and expected fears, like the US becoming involved in another world war, remain on the list, but it now sits in the No. 2 spot instead of 2025’s No. 6 slot.
Possibly the most common fears that any human could have — someone you love becoming seriously ill or dying — also remained prominent in the top 10 list.

The addition of AI makes a lot of sense in the world that we live in today, however. In the top 10 list, AI-related fears surround the technology harming both the election process (ranked third) and the economy (ranked seventh). With midterm elections right around the corner, it’s not at all surprising to see AI pop up here.
The team at Chapman commissioned NORC at the University of Chicago to survey 1,221 adults online this past April.
The study doesn’t paint AI as all bad, though. It also states that there is hope about the technology, according to Seth Benzell, assistant professor of business and economics at Chapman.
“When you frame it as AI or robots that are going to allow you to build something that you weren’t able to do before … those get people a lot more excited,” Benzell said.

AI cropped up a few more times on the list, however, including AI hurting the environment (at 43.2%), AI harming personal relationships (42%), AI replacing people in the workforce (also 42%), reporting to an AI manager at work (19.1%), having your work evaluated by AI (19.3%) and working with AI-enabled technologies (17.2%).

Other fears of technology also made the list: government tracking of personal data (48.9%), cyberterrorism (45.7%), government use of drones within the US (34.2%), technology that I don’t understand (23.5%) and technological change at work (12.6%).
Other, hardly dismissible fears that have been on people’s minds for a long time remain on the list: economic collapse, biological warfare and terrorist attacks are all incredibly valid.

articles.headline: Fallout 4: FEVer Dreams Gets Official Surprise Release
keyFacts: Bethesda and modding group kinggathcreates officially released a new Fallout 4 campaign titled FEVer Dreams.
The escape room-style dungeon features original voice actors Courtenay Taylor and Brian T. Delaney and focuses on the Forced Evolutionary Virus.
Players can download the new creation on PlayStation 5, Xbox, and PC via Bethesda's Creation platform by finding a Gutsy robot in Diamond City.
body: Bethesda just gave everyone a solid reason to boot up Fallout 4 again — even if you've already racked up hundreds of hours in the post-apocalyptic RPG and its many expansions. A new release brings back Courtenay Taylor and Brian T. Delaney, the original actors who voiced Fallout 4's protagonists. This new adventure won't be like anything else you've encountered in the wasteland, though.

You begin the adventure trapped, without any weapons and seemingly poisoned by an active strain of the Forced Evolutionary Virus. Though there are shooting elements, FEVer Dreams switches things up by offering players an escape room-style dungeon full of puzzles. It's a lore-heavy experience that promises to shed light on Fallout's notorious bioweapon. Expect some familiar faces — but with some totally new gear and weapons.
'Presented by Bethesda'

The new campaign is the work of modding group @kinggathcreates, but unlike most fan creations, FEVer Dreams was made in partnership with Bethesda. In fact, the game's description reads, "Presented by Bethesda Game Studios."

The official trailer makes FEVer Dreams look like a trippy odyssey that plays with perception, which is exactly the scenario you need when you're trapped in a facility full of Deathclaws and mini nukes. Though you have to pick one of the two protagonists, the other spouse will talk to you throughout the game. There are new characters as well, and they'll bring some heavy choices: at one point during the footage, a ghoul informs the player that only one of them can use the remaining dose of what is presumably a cure for FEV. "How do you think we should handle this?" the ghoul asks.

This might be just the thing you need to pass the time before any new Fallout projects from Bethesda or Obsidian Entertainment see the light of day. The new mod creation is accessible to PlayStation 5, Xbox, and PC users alike through Bethesda's Creation platform. After downloading it, you can begin the quest by finding a Gutsy robot in the market area of Diamond City.

articles.headline: Dig through an infested planet with your giant drill-city and try not to die while you do it in the roguelite city-builder CitaDrill
keyFacts: CitaDrill is a roguelite city-builder featuring a domed city attached to a giant drill used to dig through an infested planet.
Players gather resources by drilling blocks to construct buildings, manage status effects, and defend against giant creatures.
A playable demo is currently available on Steam, with the full game scheduled for release before the end of the year.
body: You've heard of the drill that will pierce the heavens, so introducing: the drill that is attached to an entire city that will pierce the earth. That's the concept for CitaDrill, a roguelite city-builder where the city is encased in a big ole dome, a larger than life drill attached to its base that you dig through an infested planet. It's a lot, of course, but it's got some lush pixel art and a demo you can try out for yourself as part of this Steam Next Fest, too.

When you start things off, all you have is your humble drill, and a need to dig downwards. As you do so, drilling up different kinds of blocks nets you a range of resources, all dependent on the colour of the blocks you've crushed up. In typical city building fashion you use these to build up your domed city, with different fixtures providing various bonuses. Perhaps you add in a pressure valve to reduce a pressure buildup status, or you put up some power lines to get certain buildings and modules working. You may even decide to, uh, print a worker to get some jobs done.
Watch on YouTube

Of course what this is mostly all in service of is the drilling, but while you're doing that, you also have all sorts of nasty, giant creepy crawlies to worry about that want nothing more than to munch up your city. This then begets a tower defence element, whereby you need to attach various weaponry and defences to your drill-city in order to fend off incoming baddies (which, while slower paced and less screen encompassing, does have some bullet heaven vibes). There are some nasty looking bosses to fend off too, so you won't be starved of battles.

The game also has a whole cat thing going on? I think that's just for a touch of quirkiness, though it does do that thing where a real-world meme is referenced that I don't care for all that much, especially when it has so much style. Still, not offputting enough to not give it a go. Which, as a reminder, you can do! As it has a demo for you to try out on Steam right now ahead of its release before the end of the year.

articles.headline: Founder of bankrupt Samson studio mulls how to use AI for his next attempt: 'Cutting corners in game development has a habit of coming back to bite you in the ass'
keyFacts: Liquid Swords founder Christofer Sundberg confirmed the studio's bankruptcy six months after releasing the game Samson on PC.
Sundberg stated that unpaid employees will receive payments through Sweden's wage guarantee following the studio's closure.
Sundberg announced plans to open a new studio that will utilize AI for prototyping and testing without replacing human roles.
body: Christofer Sundberg, the founder of Samson developer Liquid Swords, has confirmed the studio's closure, saying that while the console version of the game enjoyed "much greater success" than the PC release, it "wasn't enough to get the company across the finish line."

Reports over the weekend revealed that Liquid Swords had gone bankrupt just six months after the PC release of Samson, which was followed by a console launch in September. "It's been a hell of a ride and a lot of fun, even when the circumstances gave us very little to laugh about," Sundberg wrote. "Building a studio, creating Samson and releasing it on PC and consoles took an enormous amount of work from people who cared deeply about what we were making.

"The console versions met with much greater success than the PC release. We got them out, but that success wasn't enough to get the company across the finish line. Market conditions and some bad business decisions brought us here, and I own my part in that. I can look honestly at what went wrong and still be proud of what we built."

Samson wasn't especially well received when it debuted on PCs, and while post-launch updates have tightened it up, it still holds a very "mixed" rating on Steam, where just 55% of user reviews are positive, and a 51 aggregate score on Metacritic. It wasn't a MindsEye-scale mess, but Sundberg acknowledged shortly after Samson's launch that Liquid Swords "released a game with flaws."

Sundberg said in his message that discussions about how to support Samson in the future are now underway; more interestingly, he added that, with Liquid Swords gone, he plans to open a new studio. Despite the lack of the traditional cooling-off period, it's not surprising that Sundberg is staying in the game dev biz: Prior to Liquid Swords, he was the co-founder and chief creative officer at Just Cause developer Avalanche Studios.

"We make mistakes, we learn, we fall, we rise up, we move on. That's sometimes a painful process, especially when it affects people you care about, but I refuse to give up. I never give up," Sundberg wrote.

"I'll be back at it again soon and will share more about my plans for a new studio. It will be built with the current market in mind, with a solid foundation and business decisions that give the games and the people making them room to succeed. The lessons from Liquid Swords will be part of how I build it. I still love making games."
From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews
It's far too early for anything concrete, but Sundberg told PC Gamer that "starting with what we can actually sustain" is the initial goal.

"A small, experienced team, low running costs and a game we can afford to finish without needing every sales forecast to come true," Sundberg explained. "I want room to make a wrong turn, fix it, and keep going without putting the whole company at risk."

Part of that will include using AI in the development process, "to help with prototyping, repetitive production tasks and testing," Sundberg said—although he emphasized that he doesn't see the technology as a game dev panacea.

"We're not looking to replace roles with AI or treating it as a way to save money (or make money quickly), because AI is bloody expensive too. And cutting corners in game development has a habit of coming back to bite you in the ass. You need solid game development experience to make anything that isn't slop and the proofs are already out there."

Sundberg is also aware of the PR risks attached to AI use, which he believes arise primarily from bold management pronouncements about the "AI-first" future with no consideration of what dev teams actually need or what problems are being solved.

"It feels like everyone is using AI, but hardly anyone talks openly about how," he said. "I think a lot of people are still figuring out where it helps and where it creates more work. Then the bill arrives for all those tokens burned, and they realise it wasn't quite the cheap shortcut they imagined.

"I'm positive about these tools, but 'AI-first' isn't a production plan or a business strategy. You need people who understand the work well enough to know when AI helps and when to switch it off. I'd like us to talk more openly about that."

Alongside the news of Liquid Swords' bankruptcy, there were claims that employees had gone unpaid for at least two months. We have since learned that the studio's bankruptcy means those employees will be paid by Sweden's wage guarantee. Sundberg declined to comment on the possibility of compensation beyond that guarantee, but said "there are people at Liquid Swords [he] would love to work with again," although it's way too soon for any commitments.

"I still want to make games with personality, freedom and enough action to cause a small diplomatic incident," Sundberg said. "I just want the explosions on screen to be bigger than the monthly overhead.
"There's plenty of fight left in me, but the next studio needs to work without running on stubbornness alone. I can do that too, but it's quite exhausting in the long-run."

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.headline: Fortnite's Nikki Skin Sparks Debate Among Horror Fans, With Some Calling for a Boycott
keyFacts: Epic Games announced a Fortnite skin based on Nikki Freeman from the movie Obsession, sparking backlash from some players.
Critics argued that turning a character who experiences severe trauma and lack of consent into a video game skin is inappropriate.
Other players defended the inclusion, stating that the character is fictional and that purchases show appreciation rather than disrespect.
body: A vocal group of Fortnite players are calling for a boycott of Epic's battle royale game after a skin of Obsession’s Nikki Freeman, played by Inde Navarrette, sparked backlash among fans.

On October 20, Epic Games revealed that Nikki Freeman is coming to Fortnite in a special collaborative video with the character’s actress, Inde Navarrette. And while there’s no denying Obsession’s popularity — Nikki was one of the most-searched Halloween costumes on Google this year, after all — her inclusion as a purchasable skin in a video game is rubbing some fans the wrong way.
Warning: Major spoilers for Obsession below!

This uncomfortable reaction is in direct response to Nikki being the victim of Bear’s wish in Obsession . In the movie, Nikki’s body is overtaken by a malicious entity while the real Nikki is locked away in her own mind, unable to do anything but watch as the entity possessing her commits atrocities while wearing her skin.
Be careful what you wish for… Nikki is coming to Fortnite tomorrow 🪾 https://t.co/iSY6eseqVX
— Fortnite (@Fortnite) October 20, 2026

She is also taken advantage of by Bear, who engages in intimacy with Nikki’s physical form without getting the consent of the real Nikki. (Bear becomes aware of this fact in the film, but decides against trying to save her, asking, ‘What’s so bad about being with me?’ to which Nikki replies, ‘I’ve never been with you, Bear.’)

Needless to say, making Nikki — who is a victim of rape — a playable character in a video game isn’t exactly being met with positivity from some folks in Fortnite’s playerbase. That’s not including her special emote, which sees her hold up Wiley E. Coyote-style signs reenacting the famous dinner scene where she flips out on Bear, or the skin’s recreation of her iconic frown.

“Wanting your rape victim character in a game as a fun element (ironically Nikki suffers from has no control on her body and mind in movie) is a f**king choice,” one user wrote on Twitter/X. “Also, f**k Fortnite too for this choice.”
“I kind of hate how Nikki was turned into a meme like this. It kinda overshadows the actual horrific s**t her character actually went through in the movie, in my opinion,” another said .

“So, lemme [make] this make sense: Fortnite is using a character who has a narrative about loss of coercion, loss of consent, psychological torment, and tragic violence for entertainment purposes? Fortnite monopolizing on obsession gives me the ick. I'm grossed out,” another argued .

A viral post , which has since been deleted, even called for a boycott of Fortnite altogether due to the skin — but another segment of the game's playerbase isn't on board with this idea, with several arguing that Nikki is merely a fictional character and that her Fortnite skin “isn’t that deep.”

“There’s obviously heated discussion surrounding Nikki being put into Fortnite, but I don't really get how the character [being] integrated into [the] game = not taking her story seriously. Most people BUY these things BECAUSE they care about a character, it's usually not for a punchline,” one said .

“Let’s please not try to reduce Nikki to just another ‘victim,’” another asked . “Yes, her story is horrific and tragic, but that does NOT mean we shouldn’t allow for her to appear in multi-media regardless of quality.”
“People have such a hard time comprehending that Nikki isn’t a real person and that she’s a fictional character,” yet another posed .

This isn’t the first time Nikki’s inclusion in other events an IPs has sparked a debate; she was also featured as a wandering character at Universal Studios’ Halloween Horror Nights , which sparked its own discourse in the horror scene as to whether or not this was actually ethical (not to mention concerns about the actors’ safety). Indie Navarrette, for her part, seems to have no issue with the whole thing, even posing with one of the character's actors for a photo while visiting the theme park this October.

articles.headline: Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June
keyFacts: Ransomware groups including Qilin and Inc have been exploiting a high-severity PAN-OS authentication bypass bug since June, according to Unit 42.
Palo Alto Networks disclosed and patched the vulnerability on May 13 after initially assigning it a medium-severity rating.
Attackers are using the bug to establish unauthorized VPN sessions, bypass multi-factor authentication, and deploy ransomware across numerous industries.
body: Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing.
CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection.

The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation.
That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17.
On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE.

“Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42.

After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned.

In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail."
Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected.

Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators , are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions.

“The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).”
This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added.
Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27532 , which targets Veeam backup infrastructure.

So if you haven’t already patched vulnerable PAN-OS software, do so now - and investigate whether attackers have already gained access to your network. Check Unit 42’s indicators of compromise to assist with threat-hunting activities.®

articles.headline: Webb backs VAR over Botman challenge on Jackson
keyFacts: Premier League referees' chief Howard Webb backed the video assistant referee's decision not to issue a red card for Sven Botman's foul on Nicolas Jackson.
Botman received a yellow card from referee Jarred Gillett for the 18th-minute challenge during Aston Villa's 1-0 victory over Newcastle.
Webb stated that the VAR supported the on-field caution because the tackle lacked stud contact and a secondary scissor action.
body: - Published

Premier League referees' chief Howard Webb says Sven Botman's foul on Nicolas Jackson was a "high-end reckless challenge" but backed the video assistant referee's decision not to intervene for a red card.

Botman was shown a yellow card - the correct sanction for a reckless tackle - by referee Jarred Gillett for the Newcastle centre-back's 18th minute challenge on Villa striker Nicolas Jackson on Saturday.
The Dutch defender went in strongly and over the top of the ball, though contact on the opponent was with his trailing leg.
"I think it's reckless," Gillett said of the challenge. "Even though you get a touch on the ball, it's still reckless."
The VAR, Stuart Attwell, decided to support the on-field call of a caution because there was "no secondary scissor action" and contact was "not with the studs".

"I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card, but it was a yellow," Jackson said after the game. "I nearly broke my leg, but anyway, it's part of football."
Webb says the on-field decision would have remained whether Gillett showed a yellow or a red card.
Villa won the game 1-0 through a 36th-minute Johan Manzambi goal.
'Good example' of referee's call - Webb
On Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb said that "robust tackling" is "part of the English game" but that referee still had "a responsibility to ensure players' safety".
"The referee in the moment, on the ground, sees it as a reckless challenge - no doubt a high-end reckless challenge - as Botman comes in and gets a touch on the ball," Webb said.
"There's obviously some speed he comes in with. The VAR looks at that decision and tries to identify whether that was clearly wrong.
"We don't want the referee's decision to be re-refereed by the VAR. We want the referee to have ownership of the decision and the VAR to only step in when there's an element that's clearly wrong.

"So if the VAR had seen strong stud contact from Botman's extended leg into the ankle or shin of Jackson, or there had been a closing of the scissor, I think we'd have probably come out with a different outcome after the VAR had looked at it.
"But he doesn't see that. He realises it's subjective, and he allows it to stay on the field with the referee's call standing.
"Equally, if that had been a red card, for sure it would've been check complete by the VAR as well.
"So, it's a good example really of how the referee's call is working in the Premier League this season.
"A lighter-touch approach: let the referees referee the decision and the VAR step in when there's something clearly really wrong."
After seven rounds of Premier League games there have been 21 VAR interventions, with nine of those subjective. At the same point last season, there had been only three, with zero subjective.
However, mistakes are markedly down relative to the number of interventions.

This season, the Premier League Key Match Incidents Panel has judged one VAR intervention was wrong - Man City's offside winning goal at Man United - with one missed to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa.
Last season, there had been four errors for missed interventions after seven rounds.

articles.headline: Harry Enten Skewers Vance Over Latest Gas Price Excuse: 'Nobody's Buying That'
keyFacts: CNN analyst Harry Enten said Americans are rejecting JD Vance's claim blaming Joe Biden for high gas prices.
Enten cited polling data showing Vance's net favorability rating dropped 18 points to negative 15 points.
Enten concluded that Vance is currently the least popular Republican vice president at this point in a vice presidency.
body: CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten highlighted JD Vance’s abysmal approval ratings on Monday and said “nobody’s buying” the vice president’s excuse for high gas prices.

Enten appeared on “News Central” Monday with host John Berman, who played footage of Vance claiming on Saturday that former President Joe Biden, rather than Donald Trump’s costly Iran war, is to blame for skyrocketing fuel costs.

“I would just say, nobody’s buying that line of reasoning,” Enten said. “Americans think there’s a lack of reasoning in that argument. I mean, you could just see it right here. I mean, just take a look at JD Vance’s net favorability rating.”

Enten continued, “You go back to the beginning of his vice presidency, you could see it right there. He was 3 points above water. Hey, 3 points! You’re on the positive side of the ledger. But down he goes into Lake Erie, to use a nice body of water in his home state, to -15 points.”
“That’s a switcheroo, Johnny B., of 18 points in the wrong direction,” he told Berman.
Enten also noted that Vance’s “net favorability among independents has gone from about 0 — which ain’t too great but ain’t too awful — to now about -30 points with independents, going the wrong way.”

Enten cited his own aggregate and data from “various pollsters” to conclude that Vance is currently “by far, the least popular Republican vice president at this point in a vice presidency,” noting that even Dan Quayle was perceived more favorably.
“Surely he’s doing well in his home state of Ohio?” Berman asked.

“You know what, maybe you could say, ‘Yeah … surely you could send him to Ohio,’” said Enten. “Look at this, look at JD Vance’s net favorability in Ohio: He’s now even underwater there. Seven points underwater in his home state of Ohio. He’s deep under the Ohio River.”
He noted, “He, simply put, is not helpful nationally, and he’s not even helpful in his own home state.”

articles.headline: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
keyFacts: Polestar and University of Oxford researchers are studying how driving performance cars affects the human driver physically and mentally.
A pilot study tested 12 drivers on a Swedish track using heart rate monitors, electrode skullcaps, and gaze-tracking systems while driving the Polestar 4.
The study combined physiological data and car telemetry with subjective driver interviews to measure the human experience behind the wheel.
body: The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.”

A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster.

Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? That’s a question Polestar is trying to answer with researchers at the University of Oxford.

“As electric cars redefine what performance can be, we wanted to understand something that can’t be captured by a specification sheet alone: the human experience behind the wheel,” said Christian Samson, Polestar’s head of product attributes. “Working with University of Oxford allows us to look at performance through a different lens—connecting the engineering of the car with the experience of the person driving it.”

The pilot study involved 12 drivers who track-tested both rear- and all-wheel-drive versions of the Polestar 4 at a track in Sweden. The Polestar 4 is the OEM’s midsize crossover, a compelling Porsche Macan alternative that you can sadly no longer buy here in the US. The drivers were instrumented with heart rate monitors and skullcaps studded with electrodes, plus the cars’ gaze-tracking driver monitoring system to gather physiological data, which was combined with telemetry from the cars and subjective interview assessments after the fact. While being measured, drivers lapped the Gotland Ring circuit gently, then dynamically.
